issues.legal_issue: Attachment of immovable property belonging to a member of a Scheduled Tribe in execution of a money decree is invalid when the required permission has not been obtained.
material_facts: The property belonged to a judgment-debtor whom the parties treated as a member of a Scheduled Tribe.
The property was attached in execution of a money decree before permission for its attachment or sale had been obtained from the competent authority.
issues.conclusion: The attachment was void because it contravened the prohibition on attachment without the competent authority’s permission.
issues.legal_principle: Clause 6 of the Orissa Scheduled Areas Transfer of Immovable Property by Scheduled Tribes Regulation No. 2 of 1956 and Rule 4 made under it provide that immovable property belonging to a member of a Scheduled Tribe cannot be attached or sold in execution of a money decree except in accordance with permission from the competent authority.

predicates.money_decree_execution: A creditor sought to enforce a money decree against immovable property through execution proceedings.
predicates.property_belongs_to_tribal_member: The immovable property belonged to a person treated as a member of a Scheduled Tribe.
predicates.attachment_without_required_permission: The executing court attached the property without the required permission from the competent authority.

issues.definition: When a creditor seeks to enforce a money decree against property belonging to a member of a Scheduled Tribe and the property is attached without the required permission, the attachment is void.

issues.legal_issue: A court auction cannot displace a purchaser’s title acquired under an authorized private sale completed before the auction when the judgment-debtor has no saleable interest at the time of auction, and an auction that breaches a condition imposed on the authorized sale cannot confer valid title.
material_facts: The competent authority permitted the tribal owner to sell the property privately for a specified price.
The owner sold the property to the private purchaser after obtaining permission and before the court auction.
The attachment preceding the private sale was void, and the owner had no saleable interest left when the auction occurred.
The auction was conducted for less than the price required by the permission.
issues.conclusion: The auction sale was invalid and could not displace the private purchaser’s title.
issues.legal_principle: A court sale transfers only the judgment-debtor’s right, title, and interest, so an auction purchaser acquires no interest the debtor no longer has. Further, where permission for a private sale is subject to a price condition, an auction sale that violates that condition cannot confer valid title. The Court applied clause 6 of the Orissa Scheduled Areas Transfer of Immovable Property by Scheduled Tribes Regulation No. 2 of 1956 and Rule 4 made under it.

predicates.execution_auction_sale: A court auction transferred property in execution of a money decree.
predicates.prior_authorized_private_transfer: The owner transferred the property privately to a purchaser, after obtaining the competent authority’s permission and before the auction, leaving the judgment-debtor with no interest to sell.
predicates.auction_breached_sale_condition: The auction sale failed to satisfy a condition imposed by the competent authority on the permitted sale.

issues.definition: If an execution auction follows an authorized private transfer that left the judgment-debtor with no interest to sell, or the auction breaches a condition imposed on the permitted sale, the auction sale is invalid.

issues.legal_issue: A judgment-debtor’s failure to raise an objection in execution does not operate as actual or constructive res judicata against a person claiming through the judgment-debtor when the validity of the auction sale is the issue and the relevant status and need for sanction were not disputed.
material_facts: The private purchaser claimed through the judgment-debtor.
The judgment-debtor had not raised the particular objections to the auction in the execution proceedings.
Neither the judgment-debtor nor the decree-holder disputed that the judgment-debtor was a member of a Scheduled Tribe, and both were aware that sanction was needed for a sale of the property.
The decree-holder had informed the executing court that permission was needed, and the basic issue later was the validity of the auction sale.
issues.conclusion: The judgment-debtor’s failure to raise the particular objections did not operate as actual or constructive res judicata against the judgment-debtor or the purchaser claiming through him.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that no question of actual or constructive res judicata arose on these facts: the basic issue was the validity of the auction sale, the purchaser claimed through the judgment-debtor, and the judgment-debtor’s tribal status and the need for sanction had not been disputed.

rule.if: execution_sale_dispute and claimant_derives_title_from_judgment_debtor and debtor_omitted_objection and tribal_status_was_not_disputed and parties_knew_sanction_was_needed

predicates.execution_sale_dispute: The dispute concerned the validity of a court auction conducted in execution proceedings.
predicates.claimant_derives_title_from_judgment_deb: The person challenging the auction claimed title through the judgment-debtor.
predicates.debtor_omitted_objection: The judgment-debtor did not raise the particular objection to the auction in the execution proceedings.
predicates.tribal_status_was_not_disputed: The parties did not dispute that the judgment-debtor was a member of a Scheduled Tribe.
predicates.parties_knew_sanction_was_needed: The parties knew that the property could not be sold without the competent authority’s sanction.

issues.definition: In an execution-sale dispute, the debtor’s omission does not bar a later challenge by a person claiming through the debtor when tribal status was undisputed and the parties knew sanction was needed.

issues.legal_issue: A contention about whether a community falls within a scheduled tribal group cannot be raised for the first time in a second appeal or an appeal under Article 136.
material_facts: The contention that the judgment-debtor’s community did not fall within a Scheduled Tribe was based on its not being expressly named in the relevant schedule.
Whether the community fell within a scheduled subgroup was raised for the first time in the second appeal and was sought to be raised again in the appeal under Article 136.
issues.conclusion: The contention could not be raised for the first time in the second appeal and could not be raised in the appeal under Article 136.
issues.legal_principle: The Court relied on paragraph 2 of the Constitution (Scheduled Tribes) Order, 1950, which provides that tribes, parts of tribes, or groups within tribes specified in the Schedule are deemed to be Scheduled Tribes. It held that the question whether the community fell within a scheduled subgroup could not be raised for the first time in the second appeal, and still less in an appeal under Article 136.

predicates.second_appeal_or_special_leave_appeal: The matter was before a court in a second appeal or an appeal under Article 136.
predicates.tribal_classification_plea_raised_for_fi: A party first argued at that appellate stage that the person’s community did not qualify as a Scheduled Tribe or fall within a scheduled subgroup.

issues.definition: When a tribal-classification contention is raised for the first time in a second appeal or an appeal under Article 136, the new contention is not entertained.

issues.legal_issue: A decree-holder who treated the judgment-debtor as a member of a Scheduled Tribe and sought permission on that basis cannot later deny that status to argue that permission was unnecessary.
material_facts: The decree-holder sought permission from the executing court to sell the property on the stated basis that its owner was a member of a Scheduled Tribe.
The competent authority’s permission, obtained at the private purchaser’s instance, was later produced by the decree-holder in the execution proceedings as permission for the sale.
The decree-holder subsequently argued that the owner was not a member of a Scheduled Tribe and that permission was therefore unnecessary.
issues.conclusion: The decree-holder could not dispute that the owner was a member of a Scheduled Tribe or contend that permission was unnecessary.
issues.legal_principle: The Court relied on the decree-holder’s own conduct: he had sought permission on the basis of the owner’s tribal status and later used the permission in the execution proceedings. The Court held that he could not then deny that status; it cited no separate earlier case for this point.

predicates.execution_proceeding: A creditor was pursuing enforcement of a money decree through execution proceedings.
predicates.creditor_sought_permission_based_on_trib: The creditor asked the executing court to obtain permission to sell the property on the basis that its owner was a member of a Scheduled Tribe.
predicates.creditor_later_denied_tribal_status: The creditor later argued that the owner was not a member of a Scheduled Tribe and that permission was unnecessary.

issues.definition: In execution proceedings, a creditor who sought permission on the basis of the owner’s tribal status and later denied that status cannot deny it.
